explanation: The hallway camera gets its power through the hallway smart plug. At 23:00, R1 switches that plug off to save energy, which also shuts the camera down. If the home is in away mode, the camera recording that R2 started stops without notice, so the front door isn't watched overnight.
evidence: R1 turns plug_hall.power off at 23:00
AFFECTS edge: plug_hall.power == off sets camera_hall.power off (the camera is powered through the hallway smart plug)
R2 turns camera_hall.recording on when home_mode == away
Nothing in R1 checks home_mode, so it can run while the home is in away mode and R2 expects the camera to be recording
repair: Add a condition to R1 so it only turns off the hallway plug when home_mode is not away. Even better, move the camera to a power source that the energy-saving rule never switches off.

explanation: R3 locks the front door when the home switches to night mode. R4 unlocks the same door when it detects motion in the hallway between 22:00 and 06:00. Night mode and that time window will usually overlap, so any hallway movement at night (a resident walking by, a pet) can unlock the door right after night mode locked it. The door would then stay unlocked overnight.
evidence: R3 sets lock_front.lock to locked when home_mode == night
R4 sets lock_front.lock to unlocked when motion_hall == true and the time is between 22:00 and 06:00
Both rules control the same lock (lock_front.lock), and their actions are opposite (locked vs. unlocked)
Neither rule has a condition that stops both from firing at night, and R4 does not check home_mode
Hallway motion is also expected when someone sets night mode or walks around afterwards, so R4 can fire right after R3
repair: Give R4 an extra condition so it only unlocks when home_mode is not night, for example a dedicated 'guests leaving' mode. Another option is to replace the motion trigger with a deliberate action, such as an indoor unlock button. You could also have the door re-lock itself after a short delay if it is still unlocked during night mode.

explanation: R5 turns off the living room lamp at 23:00, and R2 starts the hallway camera recording when the home is set to away mode. They control different devices. Neither one changes anything the other rule depends on, and no physical link between them was found, so they can run together safely.
evidence: R5 controls only lamp_living.power (off at 23:00).
R2 controls only camera_hall.recording (on when home_mode == away).
lamp_living is in the living room and camera_hall is in the hallway, so they are separate devices.
Turning off the lamp does not change home_mode, which is the trigger for R2.
No AFFECTS edges or causal chains were retrieved that link the lamp to the camera (for example, a shared power supply or light level).
repair: none

explanation: R1 switches off the hallway smart plug at 23:00, and R3 locks the front door when the home goes into night mode. They control different devices, and nothing in the knowledge graph connects the plug, or the camera it powers, to the front door lock or to home_mode. Neither rule undoes or blocks the other, so there is no conflict between them. As a separate safety point, R1 also turns off the hallway security camera every night at 23:00. Neither rule depends on the camera, but you may still want to check this side effect.
evidence: R1 targets plug_hall.power := off at 23:00; R3 targets lock_front.lock := locked when home_mode == night
The two rules act on different devices (plug_hall vs lock_front), so their actions can't contradict each other
The only AFFECTS edge is plug_hall.power == off -> camera_hall.power off; there is no edge from the plug or the camera to lock_front or home_mode
Neither R1 nor R3 has a trigger or condition that uses camera_hall, so turning off the camera doesn't stop or start either rule
R3 doesn't change anything that R1's time trigger depends on

explanation: R1 turns on the living room heater at 18:00, and nothing ever turns it off. As the heater warms the room past 26 °C, R2 turns on the fan and opens the window. The heater then keeps running while cold outdoor air comes in, so the two rules work against each other and waste energy. The room temperature may also keep rising and falling around 26 °C.
evidence: R1 sets heater_living.power := on at 18:00, and no rule ever turns it off
heater_living.power == on AFFECTS temp_living increase (the heater warms the living room)
R2 is triggered by temp_living > 26, which the heater can reach (causal chain R1 -> temp_living -> R2)
R2 sets window_living.position := open and vent_living.power := on
window_living.position == open AFFECTS temp_living decrease (cold outdoor air during the heating season), working against the heater, which is still on
repair: Add an action to R2 that turns off heater_living when the temperature goes above 26 °C. Also add a condition to R1 so the heater only turns on when window_living.position == closed and temp_living is below a comfort setpoint, for example 22 °C. This stops the heater and the open window from running at the same time.

explanation: These two rules control different devices in different rooms. R3 turns on the bedroom heater at 21:00, and that only warms the bedroom. R2 only reacts to the living room temperature. Nothing in the home's graph links the bedroom heater to the living room temperature, and the window opened by R2 only cools the living room, so neither rule triggers or blocks the other.
evidence: R3 targets heater_bedroom.power := on, triggered by time == 21:00
R2 is triggered by temp_living > 26 and targets vent_living.power and window_living.position
heater_bedroom.power == on AFFECTS temp_bedroom (increase) only, not temp_living
window_living.position == open AFFECTS temp_living (decrease), which R3 does not depend on
The rules share no devices and no shared power or other physical link is recorded
repair: none

explanation: These two rules can set each other off. When the living room gets above 26 °C, R2 opens the window, and in the heating season that can let in enough cold air to bring the room below 19 °C. That turns on the heater through R4 while the window is still open. Neither rule ever turns the heater off or closes the window, so the heater keeps running until the room passes 26 °C again and R2 fires again. You end up heating the outdoors, wasting energy and swinging between too hot and too cold.
evidence: R2 is triggered by temp_living > 26 and sets window_living.position := open (and vent_living.power := on)
AFFECTS: window_living.position == open -> temp_living decrease (cold outdoor air during the heating season)
Causal chain: R2's open window lowers temp_living, which can reach R4's trigger temp_living < 19
R4 is triggered by temp_living < 19 and sets heater_living.power := on
AFFECTS: heater_living.power == on -> temp_living increase, which can reach R2's trigger temp_living > 26
No rule closes the window or turns off the heater, so both can be active at once and the cycle can repeat
repair: Add the condition 'window_living.position == closed' to R4 and make R4 close the window before turning on the heater. Also add the condition 'heater_living.power == off' to R2, or make R2 turn the heater off when it opens the window. This way the heater never runs with the window open.

explanation: Both rules fire at exactly 18:00. When the home is in away mode, R1 turns the living room heater on while R5 turns it off. The heater's final state depends on which rule runs last. If R1 wins, an electric space heater could run in an empty house and keep warming the living room.
evidence: R1 is TRIGGERED_BY time == 18:00 and TARGETS heater_living.power := on with no condition
R5 is TRIGGERED_BY time == 18:00, CONDITIONED_ON home_mode == away, and TARGETS heater_living.power := off
heater_living.power has states {on, off}, so 'on' and 'off' can't both hold
Whenever home_mode == away at 18:00, both rules fire at the same moment
heater_living.power == on AFFECTS temp_living increase, so the heater could heat an unoccupied room
repair: Add the condition home_mode != away to R1, so it only turns the heater on at 18:00 when someone is home. The two rules then can't both apply at the same time, and R5 will reliably keep the heater off in away mode.

explanation: At 10:00 on weekdays R1 starts the robot vacuum, often while nobody is home. The living room motion sensor picks up the moving vacuum, and that wrongly tells R2 someone is home, so R2 unlocks the entrance door. The house can end up unlocked while it's empty, which is a security risk.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 on weekdays
AFFECTS edge: vacuum.mode == cleaning sets motion_living true (the PIR sensor detects the moving vacuum)
R2 is TRIGGERED_BY motion_living == true and sets lock_entrance.lock := unlocked
Both the vacuum and the motion sensor are in the living_room
R2 has no condition that checks whether a person is actually home or whether the vacuum is cleaning
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only unlocks when vacuum.mode == docked. Better still, base R2 on confirmed presence (for example a phone geofence or an authenticated arrival) instead of PIR motion alone.

explanation: On weekdays at 10:00, R1 starts the robot vacuum, usually while everyone is out and the home is in away mode. The living room motion sensor picks up the moving vacuum, so R3 sees motion while the home is away and sounds the siren. The result is a false alarm every weekday that nobody was in the house to cause.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 on weekdays, with no condition on home mode
Knowledge graph: vacuum.mode == cleaning AFFECTS motion_living, setting it to true (the living room PIR sensor detects the moving vacuum)
The vacuum is in the living_room, the same room as the motion_living sensor
R3 is TRIGGERED_BY motion_living == true and CONDITIONED_ON home_mode == away, then sets alarm.siren := on
Weekday 10:00 is a time when the home is likely in away mode, so both rules can be active together
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it only sounds the siren when vacuum.mode == docked. A better option is to use a pet-immune motion sensor or a sensor zone that ignores the vacuum. Either way, the alarm stays armed and still covers the other sensors while the vacuum runs.

explanation: R1 starts the robot vacuum, and the moving vacuum sets off the living room motion sensor. R4 only reacts to the bedroom motion sensor, which is a different sensor in a different room. The vacuum's movement can't trigger R4, and the two rules control different devices, so they don't interfere with each other.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 on weekdays; the vacuum is in the living room.
AFFECTS edge: vacuum.mode == cleaning sets motion_living true (living room PIR sensor), not motion_bedroom.
R4 is triggered only by motion_bedroom == true (bedroom PIR sensor).
No AFFECTS edge links the vacuum to motion_bedroom.
R1 controls vacuum.mode and R4 controls light_entrance.power, so the two rules never act on the same device state.
repair: none

explanation: R1 unlocks the apartment door so people can get out when the kitchen smoke detector goes off. R2 locks the same door whenever the home switches to away mode, and it doesn't check for smoke. If the home switches to away mode during a smoke alarm (or right after one), R2 can re-lock the door that R1 unlocked for evacuation. Neither rule rules out the other's situation, so they can send opposite commands to the same lock.
evidence: R1: TRIGGERED_BY smoke_kitchen == true, TARGETS lock_door.lock := unlocked
R2: TRIGGERED_BY home_mode == away, TARGETS lock_door.lock := locked
Both rules target the same device state, lock_door.lock (locked/unlocked)
R2 has no condition on smoke_kitchen, and R1 has no condition on home_mode, so both can fire while smoke is present
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only locks the door when smoke_kitchen == false. Then away mode can't re-lock the door during a smoke event. Keep the smoke detector and R1's evacuation unlock active.

explanation: R1 turns the central air handler off when the kitchen smoke detector goes off, which helps keep smoke from spreading. R4 turns the air handler back on at 08:00 and doesn't check for smoke. If smoke is still being detected at 08:00, or is detected around that time, R4 overrides R1's safety shutdown. The air handler could then spread smoke through the apartment.
evidence: R1 sets hvac.power := off when smoke_kitchen == true
R4 sets hvac.power := on at time == 08:00 with no conditions
Both rules control the same device state (hvac.power) and set it to opposite values (off vs. on)
Nothing stops R4 from running while smoke_kitchen is true, so both rules can be active at once
repair: Add the condition smoke_kitchen == false to R4, so the air handler only turns on at 08:00 when no smoke is detected. Keep R1's smoke shutdown and door unlock exactly as they are.

explanation: These two rules control different devices, and neither one affects the other. R3 turns on the kitchen hood when the oven comes on. R2 locks the apartment door when the home switches to away mode. The hood does clear smoke from the kitchen, but neither rule reacts to smoke, so that effect can't set off or block R2.
evidence: R3 is triggered by oven.power == on and only sets hood.power := on.
R2 is triggered by home_mode == away and only sets lock_door.lock := locked.
The two rules change different devices (hood and lock_door), so their commands can't contradict each other.
The only causal link is hood.power == on -> smoke_kitchen set false, and neither rule is triggered or conditioned by smoke_kitchen.
Neither rule changes home_mode or oven.power, so neither can start the other.
repair: none

explanation: Rule R1 switches off the office plug at 00:30, and the Wi-Fi router is plugged into it, so the router loses power too. Without Wi-Fi, the garden camera can't upload to the cloud. That undoes R2, which turns cloud upload on in night mode, and night mode is almost certainly active at 00:30. Doorbell notifications also stop overnight, so you lose security coverage without any warning.
evidence: R1: at 00:30 sets plug_office.power := off
R2: when home_mode == night sets camera_garden.cloud_upload := on and camera_garden.recording := on
plug_office.power == off AFFECTS router.power set off (router is plugged into the office smart plug)
router.power == off AFFECTS camera_garden.cloud_upload set off (camera uploads over Wi-Fi)
router.power == off AFFECTS doorbell.notifications set off (notifications delivered over Wi-Fi)
00:30 falls within typical night-mode hours, so both rules are active at the same time
repair: Plug the Wi-Fi router into an outlet that is always on, not the switched office smart plug. That way R1 still cuts standby power to the desk devices, but the camera upload and doorbell notifications keep working overnight.

explanation: The router is plugged into the office smart plug. At 00:30, R1 switches that plug off to save standby power, which also shuts down the router and Wi-Fi. The doorbell sends its notifications over Wi-Fi, so after 00:30 you won't get any doorbell alerts. That happens even when R3 has turned notifications on because the home is in away mode. The garden camera's cloud upload also stops.
evidence: R1 sets plug_office.power := off every day at 00:30
plug_office.power == off AFFECTS router.power set off (the router is plugged into the office smart plug)
router.power == off AFFECTS doorbell.notifications set off (notifications are delivered over Wi-Fi)
R3 sets doorbell.notifications := on when home_mode == away
router.power == off also AFFECTS camera_garden.cloud_upload set off
R1 has no condition on home_mode, so it also runs while the home is in away mode
repair: Plug the router into an always-on outlet that the office plug doesn't control. If that's not possible, add a condition to R1 so it only switches the plug off when home_mode is not away.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R4 only turns off the desk lamp plug in the office at 00:30. R2 only turns on cloud upload and recording on the garden camera when the home is in night mode. They control different devices, and neither changes anything the other rule depends on. The knowledge graph shows no link that would make the desk lamp plug affect the camera or its network connection. The home's name mentions a "network dependency chain," so if this plug actually powers something else, such as a router or modem, check this again.
evidence: R4 only targets plug_desk_lamp.power := off and is triggered by time == 00:30
R2 only targets camera_garden.cloud_upload := on and camera_garden.recording := on and is triggered by home_mode == night
plug_desk_lamp is described as 'Smart plug for the desk lamp' in the office, not as powering any network equipment
No AFFECTS edges or causal chains were found linking plug_desk_lamp to camera_garden or to network connectivity
Neither rule changes home_mode or the time, so neither can trigger or block the other

explanation: R4 turns off the desk lamp plug at 00:30. R3 turns on doorbell notifications when the home goes into away mode. They control different devices. Neither one changes anything the other rule depends on, and the knowledge graph shows no physical link between the lamp plug and the doorbell, so they can run together safely.
evidence: R4 only targets plug_desk_lamp.power (set to off) and is triggered by the time 00:30
R3 only targets doorbell.notifications (set to on) and is triggered by home_mode == away
plug_desk_lamp is in the office; doorbell is a Wi-Fi video doorbell at the entrance — different devices
No AFFECTS edges or causal chains were retrieved linking the desk lamp plug to the doorbell, home_mode, or network equipment
Neither rule's action modifies time or home_mode, the triggers of the other rule

explanation: The aquarium heater and pump are plugged into the living room power strip. When R1 switches the strip off at night, the heater and pump both lose power. After that, R2 can still "turn on" the heater when the water drops below 24 C, but nothing happens because the strip has no power. The water can keep cooling all night with no filtering or oxygen, which can harm the fish.
evidence: R1 sets strip_living.power := off when home_mode == night
AFFECTS: strip_living.power == off sets aquarium_heater.power off (heater is plugged into the strip)
AFFECTS: strip_living.power == off sets aquarium_pump.power off (pump is plugged into the strip)
R2 sets aquarium_heater.power := on when water_temp < 24, but the heater cannot run while the strip is off
Night is often when the room cools, so water_temp < 24 is likely to happen while night mode is on
repair: Plug the aquarium heater and pump into an always-on outlet, or a socket on the strip that is never switched, separate from the TV standby devices. Then R1 only cuts power to the entertainment devices. Until you can re-wire, add a condition to R1 so it only turns the strip off when aquarium_heater and aquarium_pump are not connected to it.

explanation: R3 turns off the TV smart plug at night, and that only powers down the TV. R2 turns on the aquarium heater when the water gets cold, and that only warms the water. The heater isn't plugged into the TV plug, and neither rule changes anything the other rule depends on. So both can run together safely, and the aquarium keeps its heating at night.
evidence: R3 targets plug_tv.power := off; the only downstream effect is tv.power set off (the TV is plugged into plug_tv).
R2 targets aquarium_heater.power := on; the only downstream effect is water_temp increase.
No AFFECTS edge connects plug_tv to aquarium_heater, so the heater does not draw power through the TV plug.
R2 is triggered by water_temp and R3 by home_mode. Neither rule's action changes the other rule's trigger variable.
The rules act on different devices (plug_tv/tv vs. aquarium_heater), so they can't issue opposite commands to the same device.
repair: none

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. Together they work like a normal thermostat: the heater turns on below 24 °C and off above 28 °C. The two conditions can't both be true at once, so the rules never send opposite commands at the same time. R2's heating does eventually cause R4 to fire, but that is the intended result. The 4 °C gap between the two thresholds also keeps the heater from switching on and off rapidly.
evidence: R2 fires only when water_temp < 24 and sets aquarium_heater.power := on
R4 fires only when water_temp > 28 and sets aquarium_heater.power := off
The trigger ranges (< 24 and > 28) don't overlap, so the opposite commands can never apply at the same time
AFFECTS edge: heater on -> water_temp increase, which reaches R4's trigger. This is the intended shut-off, not an unexpected side effect
The 24-28 °C gap acts as a hysteresis band that prevents rapid on/off switching
repair: none

explanation: R5 turns the aquarium heater off when the home goes into night mode. R2 turns the same heater on whenever the water drops below 24 °C. Once the heater is off, the water cools and R2 switches it back on. If night mode is entered or re-sent again, R5 turns it off again. The heater keeps flipping on and off, and the fish may spend the night in water that is too cold.
evidence: R5: TRIGGERED_BY home_mode == night, TARGETS aquarium_heater.power := off
R2: TRIGGERED_BY water_temp < 24, TARGETS aquarium_heater.power := on
Both rules set the same state, aquarium_heater.power, to opposite values (off vs on)
Neither rule has a condition that stops it firing when the other one does: night mode and water below 24 °C can happen at the same time
AFFECTS: aquarium_heater.power == on --> water_temp increase, so with the heater off at night the water cools and R2 fires
repair: Add a condition to R5 so it only turns the heater off when water_temp >= 24 (or a small margin above, such as 25 °C). Also give R2 priority so the heater can always come back on to protect the fish. A better option is to have R5 lower the heater's setpoint at night (for example to 24 °C) rather than cutting power completely.

explanation: Water for the garden sprinklers runs through the main water valve. When you're away, R1 closes that valve. R2 still starts watering at 06:00 every day, but no water can reach the sprinklers. So the controller says it's watering while the garden stays dry, and nothing tells you about it.
evidence: R1: when home_mode == away, sets valve_main.state := closed
R2: at 06:00 daily, sets irrigation.flow := on and irrigation.watering := on, with no condition on home mode or valve state
AFFECTS edge: valve_main.state == closed -> irrigation.flow set off ('The irrigation line is supplied through the main water valve')
R2 has no time or mode restriction, so it can fire while the home is in away mode and the valve is closed
Causal chain: R1's valve closure reaches irrigation.flow, which R2 sets to on
repair: Keep R1's leak protection as it is. Add a condition to R2 so it only runs when valve_main.state == open (or home_mode != away). If it's skipped, send a notification so you know the garden wasn't watered. If the garden must be watered while you're away, put the irrigation line on its own supply with a separate leak-protected valve, so the main valve can stay closed.

explanation: R2 starts watering at 06:00, which raises soil moisture until R4 fires and stops it. R4 only turns off 'watering' and leaves 'flow' on. R2 also never checks moisture, so it waters soil that is already wet. In that case R4 may never fire, because it only fires when moisture rises above 60 %.
evidence: R2 sets irrigation.flow := on and irrigation.watering := on at 06:00
R4 is triggered by soil_moisture > 60 and sets only irrigation.watering := off
AFFECTS: irrigation.watering == on -> soil_moisture increase
Causal chain: R2's action reaches R4's trigger (soil_moisture > 60)
R2 has no soil-moisture condition; R4 never resets irrigation.flow
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only runs when soil_moisture <= 60, and make R4 turn off both irrigation.watering and irrigation.flow (optionally stop at a slightly higher level, e.g. 62 %, so it doesn't switch on and off around 60 %).

explanation: R5 closes the outdoor tap valve when the home goes into away mode, and R2 starts the garden sprinkler at 06:00. They control different devices, and the knowledge graph describes the tap valve as a separate line with no physical link to the sprinkler. Watering only raises soil moisture, and neither rule uses that. So neither rule undoes, blocks or triggers the other.
evidence: R5 targets valve_garden.state := closed; R2 targets irrigation.flow and irrigation.watering := on, so the two rules control different devices
valve_garden is described as a 'Separate valve on the outdoor tap line'
No AFFECTS edge links valve_garden to the irrigation controller's water supply
R2's only causal effect is a rise in soil_moisture, which no rule uses as a trigger or condition
R2 does not change home_mode, R5's trigger
repair: none

explanation: The two rules control different devices, so they never give opposite commands to the same device. The conflict comes through the light sensor they share. When strong sun pushes the living room above 800 lux, R1 closes the blinds. Closed blinds block daylight, so the reading can fall below 150 lux, and then R2 turns on the ceiling lights in the middle of a sunny day. Nothing in these rules opens the blinds again, so the room can stay with blinds closed and lights on. It could also loop the other way: if the lights alone push the reading above 800 lux, R1 fires again. That is less likely, because ceiling lights rarely get that bright.
evidence: R1: TRIGGERED_BY lux_living > 800, TARGETS blinds_living.position := closed
R2: TRIGGERED_BY lux_living < 150, TARGETS lights_living.power := on
AFFECTS edge: blinds_living.position == closed -> lux_living decrease ('Closed blinds block daylight')
AFFECTS edge: lights_living.power == on -> lux_living increase ('Ceiling lights raise the illuminance measured by the sensor')
Causal chain: R1 action reaches the trigger of R2 (lux_living < 150); R2 action reaches the trigger of R1 (lux_living > 800)
Both rules read the same sensor (lux_living), and neither rule has a condition that blocks this chain
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only turns on the lights when the blinds are open or it is after sunset. Then darkness caused by R1 closing the blinds during the day will not switch the lights on. Optionally, also lower R1's closing level to a partly-open setting (if the blinds support it), or add a rule that reopens the blinds when the lux level drops back to normal.

explanation: R3 opens the living room blinds at 07:30 and R4 closes them at 22:00. Both rules control the same blinds, but they run at different times that never overlap, so they can't fight over the blinds. Closing the blinds makes the living room darker, but no rule here reacts to light level, so nothing else is set off.
evidence: R3 is triggered only at time == 07:30 and sets blinds_living.position := open
R4 is triggered only at time == 22:00 and sets blinds_living.position := closed
The two triggers are separate times of day, so the rules can never fire at the same moment
Closing the blinds lowers lux_living (Closed blinds block daylight), but neither R3 nor R4 depends on lux_living
Neither rule has a condition that the other rule's action could change
repair: none

explanation: R1 closes the living room blinds, which only lowers the light level in the living room. R5 turns on the study desk light, and it only reacts to the study's light level. Nothing in this home links the living room blinds to the light in the study. The two rules control different devices in different rooms, so they can't send opposite commands or set each other off.
evidence: R1 is triggered by lux_living > 800 and sets blinds_living.position := closed (living_room).
R5 is triggered by lux_study < 150 and sets lights_study.power := on (study).
The only AFFECTS edge is blinds_living closed -> lux_living decrease; it does not reach lux_study.
Causal chain for R1 ends at lux_living, which R5 does not depend on.
The two rules control different devices (blinds_living vs lights_study), so they cannot give opposite commands to the same device.
repair: none

explanation: At 07:30, R3 opens the living room blinds. On a sunny morning, opening them lets in daylight, so the room's brightness can go above 800 lux, which makes R1 close the blinds again. Both rules can run within minutes of each other and set the same blinds to opposite positions, so the blinds open and then shut almost straight away. R1 then makes the room darker, so R1 won't fire again until the light rises above 800 lux once more.
evidence: R3 sets blinds_living.position := open at 07:30
R1 sets blinds_living.position := closed when lux_living > 800
Both rules control the same device state, blinds_living.position, and set it to opposite values (open vs. closed)
AFFECTS: blinds_living.position == closed causes lux_living to decrease, so opening the blinds is likely to raise lux_living (assumed: the graph only lists the 'closed' effect)
No condition stops R3 when the room is already bright or when R1 has just closed the blinds for glare
repair: Make R1's glare protection win. Add a condition to R3 so it only opens the blinds if the outdoor or window-side light level is below the glare threshold (800 lux). If you don't have an outdoor light sensor, you could instead have R3 open the blinds only partway on bright mornings.

explanation: At 20:00, R1 turns on the nursery humidifier, which raises the room's humidity. Once humidity goes above 55 %, R2 turns on the dehumidifier. Since nothing turns the humidifier off, both machines run against each other all night. That wastes energy and makes the nursery's humidity unstable.
evidence: R1: TRIGGERED_BY time == 20:00, TARGETS humidifier_nursery.power := on
humidifier_nursery.power == on AFFECTS humidity_nursery increase
R2: TRIGGERED_BY humidity_nursery > 55, TARGETS dehumidifier_nursery.power := on
dehumidifier_nursery.power == on AFFECTS humidity_nursery decrease
Causal chain: R1's action reaches R2's trigger (humidity_nursery > 55)
Neither rule turns the other device off, so both can run at the same time

evidence: R1: home_mode == night -> strip_living.power := off
R2: water_temp < 24 -> aquarium_heater.power := on

explanation: When the home is in away mode, R1 closes the main water valve. The garden sprinklers get their water through that valve, so when R2 turns the sprinklers on at 06:00 no water can flow. repair: Decide on purpose what should happen while you are away. Option 1: add the condition home_mode != away to R2 and tell the household that watering stops in away mode. explanation: Here's how these two rules interact. R2 starts the sprinkler at 06:00, which raises the soil moisture. R4 only turns off 'watering' and leaves 'flow' on, so water may keep running through the controller. R4 also only reacts when the reading rises past 60%. If the soil is already wetter than 60% at 06:00, R2 starts watering anyway, R4 never fires, and the garden can be overwatered with no stop at all.

Knowledge graph: irrigation.watering == on raises soil_moisture
Causal chain: R2's action reaches soil_moisture > 60, which triggers R4
R4 sets only irrigation.watering := off; irrigation.flow is never turned off

repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only starts at 06:00 when soil_moisture <= 60. Also change R4 so it sets both irrigation.watering := off and irrigation.flow := off. Optionally, add a maximum watering time as a backup stop.

explanation: On a bright day, R1 closes the living room blinds to cut glare. Closed roller blinds block daylight, so the light level can drop below 150 lux. R2: lux_living < 150 -> lights_living.power := on

AFFECTS: lights_living.power == on -> lux_living increase, which reaches R1's trigger (lux_living > 800)

explanation: At 20:00, R1 turns on the nursery humidifier, which raises the room's humidity. Nothing in R1 limits how high the humidity can go, so it can rise above 55%. That triggers R2, which turns on the dehumidifier. Both machines then run at the same time and work against each other. This wastes energy, makes the humidity swing up and down, and the baby gets neither the humid air you wanted nor reliable mould protection.
evidence: R1: TRIGGERED_BY time == 20:00, TARGETS humidifier_nursery.power := on

R2: TRIGGERED_BY humidity_nursery > 55, TARGETS dehumidifier_nursery.power := on
dehumidifier_nursery.power == on AFFECTS humidity_nursery decrease

Neither rule turns the other device off or limits the humidifier to a humidity target

Also change R2 so it turns the humidifier off first, before turning the dehumidifier on. This way the two machines never run at the same time.

The fan lowering the humidity until R4 switches it off is what these rules are meant to do, not an unexpected side effect. The 20-point gap also keeps the fan from rapidly switching on and off.
evidence: R3 triggers on humidity_bath > 70 and sets fan_bath.power := on

explanation: R2 turns the nursery dehumidifier on whenever humidity exceeds 55 %, while R5 turns it off at 20:00 for quiet sleep. R5: TRIGGERED_BY time == 20:00, TARGETS dehumidifier_nursery.power := off

explanation: R1 and R2 give the same thermostat opposite instructions during overlapping times. R1 sets it to heat at 23 °C at 18:00. R2 TARGETS thermostat.mode := eco and thermostat.setpoint := 19, TRIGGERED_BY home_mode == home

Once R3 turns the AC to cooling, nothing turns it off again, so the room can drop below 20 C. That makes R4 switch on the heating while the AC is still cooling. R5 is triggered only at time == 08:00 and sets thermostat.mode := eco

R1's causal effect (temp_living increase) does not feed any trigger or condition of R5, since R5 depends only on time

explanation: When the home goes into away mode, R1 switches off the garage circuit breaker. The garage exhaust fan is on that circuit, so it loses power too. If carbon monoxide is then detected in the garage, R2 tries to turn on the exhaust fan, but the fan has no power and can't run. R2: co_garage == true -> fan_garage.power := on and garage_door.position := open

R1 has no condition that excludes CO being detected while the home is in away mode

As a further safeguard, have R2 first switch breaker_garage.power back on before it turns on the fan.

explanation: When CO is detected, R2 opens the garage door to let fresh air in. R3 closes that same door whenever the home switches to away mode. If both happen together, for example a car is left running as everyone leaves, the door ends up closed and CO builds up in the garage. That defeats the safety ventilation.
evidence: R2 TARGETS garage_door.position := open when co_garage == true
R3 TARGETS garage_door.position := closed when home_mode == away
R3 has no condition that checks co_garage, so it can fire while CO is present
co_garage and home_mode are independent variables, so both triggers can be active at the same time
repair: Add the condition co_garage == false to R3, so the garage door only closes in away mode when no CO is detected. Also make the CO response take priority, so the door reopens or stays open while CO is present.

explanation: R4 starts EV charging when the car is parked in the garage. R1 switches off the garage circuit breaker whenever the home goes into away mode. R4: car_present == true -> ev_charger.charging := on

explanation: At noon, R1 makes the feeder dispense food. The cat runs to the feeder, and that sets off the kitchen motion sensor. AFFECTS edge: feeder.dispensing == on sets motion_kitchen to true (the cat runs to the feeder)
R2 is triggered by motion_kitchen == true and turns on alarm.siren when home_mode == away
The feeder and the motion sensor are both in the kitchen

explanation: Every day at 12:00, R1 makes the feeder dispense food. Your cat then runs to the feeder in the kitchen, which sets off the kitchen motion sensor. That motion triggers R3, so the kitchen camera starts recording because of the cat, not because of an intruder or another real event. You get a daily false recording at noon, plus storage use and alerts that can make you ignore the camera.

R3 is triggered by motion_kitchen == true and sets camera_kitchen.recording := on

Chain from the knowledge graph: R1 action -> motion_kitchen = true -> R3 trigger

Either use person detection or a pet-immune motion sensor as R3's trigger, or add a condition to R3 that ignores kitchen motion for a few minutes after the feeder dispenses (for example 12:00–12:10). If you use the time window, keep the camera running in away or security mode so it still covers real events.

explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R4 runs the litter box cleaning cycle in the bathroom at noon. R5 sounds the living-room siren when motion is detected while the home is in away mode. They control different devices, and nothing R4 does changes living-room motion or the home mode.
evidence: R4 targets litter_box.cleaning (bathroom); R5 targets alarm.siren (living_room) - different devices
R5 is triggered by motion_living and conditioned on home_mode; R4's action changes neither variable
Litter box is in the bathroom, while the motion sensor is in the living room
No AFFECTS edges or causal chains were retrieved linking the litter box to motion_living or the alarm

evidence: R3 is TRIGGERED_BY motion_kitchen == true and has no condition
R6 is TRIGGERED_BY motion_kitchen == true and CONDITIONED_ON home_mode == home
R3 sets camera_kitchen.recording := on, while R6 sets camera_kitchen.recording := off
When home_mode == home, one kitchen motion event fires both rules at once

explanation: The CPAP breathing machine is plugged into the bedside smart plug, even though R1 describes that plug as the phone charger. evidence: R1 turns plug_bedside.power off at 23:30 every night

explanation: R3 unlocks the entrance door when a fall is detected so paramedics can get in. R4 locks the same door when the home switches to night mode. R4 sets lock_entrance.lock := locked when home_mode == night

The garden won't be watered even though the system reports watering as on, and a pump could run dry. Opening the valve to allow watering would remove leak protection while you're away.

R2: time == 06:00 -> irrigation.watering := on; irrigation.flow := on (no conditions on valve state or home mode)
Both can be active together: if the home is in away mode at 06:00, R2 fires while the main valve is closed
Irrigation water passes through the main water valve, a physical dependency that neither rule states
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only runs when valve_main.state == open (or home_mode != away), and send a notification when watering is skipped. Leave R1's leak protection unchanged. If you need watering while away, put the irrigation on its own valve that R1 doesn't close.

explanation: R2 turns watering on at 06:00 every day without checking the soil, and R4 turns it off when soil moisture is above 60 %. If the soil is already wet at 06:00, the two rules give opposite commands to irrigation.watering. R4 may also never fire, because it reacts to moisture crossing 60 % and the soil is already past that point, so the garden could be watered when it's already wet. R4 also only switches off irrigation.watering and leaves irrigation.flow on. In a home set up for leak protection, that means water can keep running.
evidence: R2 sets irrigation.watering := on and irrigation.flow := on at 06:00 with no conditions
R4 sets irrigation.watering := off when soil_moisture > 60, with no conditions
R2 has no soil-moisture check, so it can start watering when moisture is already above 60 %
R4's trigger is the moisture value crossing 60 %, so it may not fire again if moisture is already above 60 % when R2 starts watering
R4 does not reset irrigation.flow, so flow stays on after watering is stopped
The home is set up for irrigation and leak protection, so running water is a risk
repair: Add the condition soil_moisture <= 60 to R2 so it only starts watering when the soil is dry. Also have R4 set irrigation.flow := off along with irrigation.watering := off.

explanation: Your garden irrigation most likely gets its water through the outdoor tap valve, though neither rule says so. When the house is in away mode, R5 closes that valve. R2 then still turns watering and flow on at 06:00 every day. The watering won't actually happen, and the controller or pump may run against a closed or dry line.
evidence: R5 sets valve_garden.state := closed whenever home_mode == away.
R2 sets irrigation.watering := on and irrigation.flow := on at 06:00 daily, with no conditions.
R2 does not check home mode or the valve state, so it still fires while the home is in away mode.
In this kind of setup, the irrigation system is normally fed by the outdoor/garden tap valve. That hidden dependency means closing the valve cuts off R2's water supply.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only runs when valve_garden.state == open (or home_mode != away). Keep R5's leak protection as it is. If the garden needs watering while you're away, give the irrigation line its own supervised valve that opens only while watering is running.

explanation: On a bright day, R1 closes the living room blinds to cut glare. With the blinds closed, the room can get darker than 150 lux, and that makes R2 turn on the ceiling lights in the middle of the day. Sunlight gets swapped for electric light, which wastes energy and works against the point of using daylight. The two rules control different devices, so they never give opposite commands. The problem is that R1 changes the light level that R2 watches.
evidence: R1 action: blinds_living.position := closed when lux_living > 800
Closing the blinds cuts the daylight coming into the living room, so lux_living drops
R2 trigger: lux_living < 150, with no conditions, turns lights_living.power := on
Both rules use the same sensor (lux_living), so R1's action can directly make R2 fire
Neither rule checks the blinds position or the time of day
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only turns on the lights when the blinds are open or it is after sunset (blinds_living.position != closed OR sun below horizon). Another option is to have R1 tilt or partly close the blinds instead of closing them fully, so enough daylight stays above 150 lux.

explanation: R3 opens the living room blinds at 07:30 and R4 closes them at 22:00. Both rules control the same blinds, but they fire at different times that never overlap, so they can't give opposite commands at once. Together they just set a normal daily open/close routine. Neither rule depends on light, temperature or presence, so neither one can set off or block the other.
evidence: R3 trigger: time == 07:30, action: blinds_living.position := open
R4 trigger: time == 22:00, action: blinds_living.position := closed
The triggers are separate times of day and can never fire together
Neither rule has conditions that the other rule's action could change
repair: none

explanation: R1 closes the living room blinds when that room is bright. R5 turns on the study desk light when the study is dark. Each rule works on a different device in a different room and reads a different light sensor. Closing the living room blinds doesn't change the study's light level, and the study lamp doesn't change the living room's, so neither rule can set off or block the other.
evidence: R1 controls blinds_living and is triggered by lux_living > 800 (living room sensor).
R5 controls lights_study and is triggered by lux_study < 150 (study sensor).
The two rules don't share an actuator, so their actions can't contradict each other.
R1's action changes light in the living room only. R5 reads the study sensor, and nothing links the study's light level to the living room blinds.
R5's action adds light to the study only. R1 reads the living room sensor, so the study lamp can't trigger it.
repair: none

explanation: At 07:30, R3 opens the living room blinds and lets daylight in. On a bright morning this can push the living room above 800 lux, which fires R1 and closes the blinds again. So the morning opening can be undone within minutes. Neither rule checks what the other one did.
evidence: R3 sets blinds_living.position := open at 07:30 with no conditions
R1 sets blinds_living.position := closed whenever lux_living > 800, with no conditions
Opening blinds lets in daylight, which raises lux_living (this home's setup is daylight, blinds and lights)
Both rules act on the same device (blinds_living) with opposite target positions
Neither rule has a condition that checks current brightness or the other rule's state
repair: Add a condition to R3: only open the blinds at 07:30 if lux_living is 800 or less. Another option is to have R3 open the blinds partway (for example 50%) instead of fully, and to give R1 a hysteresis/delay (for example, lux > 800 sustained for 10 minutes) so a short burst of morning light doesn't close the blinds right away.

explanation: At 20:00, R1 turns on the nursery humidifier, which raises the humidity in the room. When humidity goes above 55 %, R2 turns on the dehumidifier in the same room. Neither rule turns its device off, so both machines can end up running against each other all night. This wastes energy and makes the nursery humidity swing up and down instead of staying steady.
evidence: R1 turns on humidifier_nursery.power at 20:00 with no conditions and no upper humidity limit.
A humidifier raises the room's humidity (humidity_nursery).
R2 is triggered by humidity_nursery > 55 and turns on dehumidifier_nursery.power.
Both devices are in the same room (the nursery) and act on the same humidity variable in opposite directions.
Neither rule turns the other device off, so both can run at the same time.
repair: Give the humidifier an upper limit: add a rule that turns humidifier_nursery off when humidity_nursery reaches about 50 %. Then add the condition humidifier_nursery.power == off to R2, so R2 also turns the humidifier off before starting the dehumidifier. This way the two devices never run at the same time.

explanation: R3 turns the bathroom fan on when humidity goes above 70 % and R4 turns it off when humidity drops below 50 %. Humidity can't be above 70 % and below 50 % at the same moment, so the two rules never fire together. The 20-point gap between them stops the fan from rapidly switching on and off. The fan lowers the humidity, which is the intended way R4 ends up switching it off. That is not an unexpected side effect.
evidence: R3 trigger: humidity_bath > 70 → fan_bath.power := on
R4 trigger: humidity_bath < 50 → fan_bath.power := off
The trigger ranges (>70 and <50) can't both be true at once
The 50–70 % gap stops the fan from rapidly switching on and off
Both rules act only on fan_bath and don't affect any other device or rule

The nursery humidifier only adds moisture to the nursery. Nothing in this home links that to the bathroom humidity sensor, so R1 shouldn't set off R3 or stop it from running.

The rules don't share any devices, and neither depends on the other for power.

explanation: Both rules control the nursery dehumidifier's power, and they set it to opposite states. R5 turns it off at 20:00 so the baby can sleep. If humidity is already high at 20:00, the dehumidifier may also switch off and then straight back on.
evidence: R2 sets dehumidifier_nursery.power := on whenever humidity_nursery > 55, with no conditions (it can fire at any time of day).
R5 sets dehumidifier_nursery.power := off at 20:00, with no conditions.

Nothing stops R2 from firing after 20:00, so it can override R5's quiet-for-sleep intent.
repair: Add a time condition to R2 so it only runs during the day (e.g., time between 07:00 and 20:00). For mould prevention at night, use a quiet or low-fan night mode, or briefly ventilate the room before 20:00.

explanation: The bedroom smart bulb gets its power through the bedroom wall switch. When night mode starts, R1 turns that switch off, which cuts power to the bulb. When the alarm rings the next morning, R2 tries to fade the bulb in to 60%, but nothing in the rules turns the switch back on first. R2 sets bulb_bedroom.power := on and brightness := 60 when alarm_clock == True, without turning switch_bedroom on
A morning alarm normally rings after night mode has started, while the switch is still off
repair: Make R2 turn switch_bedroom.power on first, then wait a few seconds for the bulb to start up before setting it to on at 60%. Another option is to change R1 so it turns off bulb_bedroom itself and leaves the wall switch powered.

explanation: The two rules control the same corridor bulb but act at different moments. R3 turns it off when the home switches into night mode, and R4 turns it on at 06:30. Each fires once on a single event and doesn't check a lasting condition, so they run one after the other (off at bedtime, on in the morning) and never fight over the bulb. Neither rule changes anything the other depends on, and neither touches the wall switch that powers the bulb.
evidence: R3 fires only when the home switches to night mode and sets bulb_corridor.power := off.
R4 fires only at time == 06:30 and sets bulb_corridor.power := on.
Neither rule has conditions, and neither checks a state that the other rule's action changes.
Neither rule controls the smart wall switch that powers the bulbs, so neither cuts power the other relies on.

Neither action changes anything the other rule depends on: R4 fires on a time and R1 fires on night mode. R4 acts on bulb_corridor.power (on) at 06:30.
The two rules control different devices in different rooms (bedroom vs. corridor).
Nothing says the corridor bulb is wired behind the bedroom wall switch.
Neither action changes home_mode or the time, so neither rule triggers or blocks the other.

explanation: Both rules control the same thermostat and their times overlap. R1 sets it to 23 °C in heat mode at 18:00. R2 sets it to 19 °C in eco mode whenever someone arrives between 17:00 and 19:00. If someone gets home between 18:00 and 19:00, R2 undoes R1's setting. If someone arrives just before 18:00, R1 undoes theirs. Which setting you end up with depends only on timing, so the thermostat can switch back and forth.
evidence: R1 sets thermostat.setpoint := 23 and thermostat.mode := heat at 18:00
R2 sets thermostat.setpoint := 19 and thermostat.mode := eco when home_mode becomes home
R2 runs at any time from 17:00 to 19:00, which includes R1's 18:00 trigger
The two rules give different values for the same setpoint and mode, and neither rule takes priority
repair: Make the time windows not overlap: change R2's window to 17:00–17:59 so it only runs before R1, or add a condition to R2 so it skips if R1 has already set heat mode to 23 °C. Alternatively, agree on one evening setpoint and keep only the rule that sets it.

explanation: R3 and R4 never fire at the same moment because their temperature triggers don't overlap, but neither rule ever switches its device off. The air conditioner can keep cooling until the room drops below 20 C, which fires R4 and turns heating on while the AC is still cooling. The AC and the heating then work against each other in the same room, wasting energy and making the temperature swing.
evidence: R3 sets ac_living.mode := cool when temp_living > 24 and never sets it back
R4 sets thermostat.mode := heat when temp_living < 20 and never sets it back
Both rules act on the same variable, temp_living, through different devices (ac_living and thermostat)
Cooling lowers temp_living and can push it below 20, which fires R4 while the AC is still in cool mode
Neither rule has a condition that checks what the other device is doing
repair: Make each rule switch the other system off: when R3 sets ac_living to cool, also set thermostat.mode := off; when R4 sets the thermostat to heat, also set ac_living.mode := off. Optionally, add a rule that turns both off once temp_living is back between 20 and 24 C.

explanation: R1 and R5 both control the thermostat, but they run at different fixed times, 18:00 and 08:00, so they can never fire at the same moment. Together they make a normal daily schedule: heating to 23 °C in the evening and eco mode in the morning. Each rule simply replaces the setting left by the other.
evidence: R1 triggers only at time == 18:00 and sets thermostat.setpoint := 23 and thermostat.mode := heat
R5 triggers only at time == 08:00 and sets thermostat.mode := eco
The trigger times are 10 hours apart, so the rules never fire together
Neither rule has conditions that depend on a temperature or other value the other rule changes, so there is no semantic chain
No power or device dependency between the rules is stated, so there is no physical conflict

explanation: R1 turns off the garage circuit breaker whenever the home goes into away mode. That breaker most likely powers the garage exhaust fan and the garage door opener, and maybe the CO sensor too. If carbon monoxide builds up while you're away, R2 will still fire, but the fan and door have no power, so the garage won't be ventilated. Nothing in either rule mentions this power dependency, which makes it a hidden safety risk.
evidence: R1 action: breaker_garage.power := off when home_mode == away
R2 relies on fan_garage.power := on and garage_door.position := open, both garage devices that probably run on the garage circuit
R2 has no conditions, so it's meant to fire any time CO is detected, including in away mode
R1 has no condition that excludes safety loads or checks CO status
The home has an EV charger and a garage door, so garage devices are probably on the garage breaker
repair: Wire the exhaust fan, garage door opener and CO sensor to a circuit that is always on, separate from the switchable garage breaker. Then R1 only cuts power to things that aren't needed for safety, like the EV charger and outlets. If rewiring isn't possible right away, add this step at the start of R2: turn breaker_garage.power on first.

explanation: R2 opens the garage door to vent carbon monoxide, and R3 closes the same door when the home goes into away mode. Neither rule checks the other's situation, so both can fire at once. For example, CO might still be present when everyone leaves, or the home might already be in away mode when CO is detected. If R3 runs after R2, the door closes, CO stays trapped in the garage, and the safety ventilation fails.
evidence: R2 action: garage_door.position := open when co_garage == True
R3 action: garage_door.position := closed when home_mode == away
Neither rule has any conditions, so nothing stops them from firing together
The home has a garage with EV charging and a garage door, so people leave from the garage and could switch to away mode while CO is present
repair: Add the condition co_garage == False to R3, so the door only closes in away mode when no CO is detected. Also give R2 priority so it reopens the door if CO is detected after the door has closed.

explanation: The EV charger in the garage is most likely powered by the garage circuit breaker, though neither rule says so. If the car is parked and charging when the home switches to away mode, R1 turns the breaker off. That cuts power to the charger and stops the charging R4 started. The rules don't show this link, so the car can be left uncharged without any warning.
evidence: R1 sets breaker_garage.power to off when home_mode becomes away, with no conditions.
R4 sets ev_charger.charging to on when car_present is True, with no conditions.
The home is described as a 'House with garage - EV charging', so the EV charger is in the garage and likely on the garage circuit.
The car can be parked in the garage (car_present == True) while the household is away, for example if people leave on foot or in another car. That makes both rules active at the same time.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so the garage breaker only turns off when ev_charger.charging is off or car_present is False. Another option is to move the EV charger to its own circuit that R1 doesn't control.

explanation: R4 and R5 both run when the car is parked in the garage, but each one controls a different device: R4 starts the EV charger and R5 turns on the garage light. Both rules only switch things on, so their actions don't contradict each other. Neither action changes anything the other rule depends on, such as car presence. Nothing in the home description says the two devices share a power supply, so there is no known physical link between them.
evidence: R4 trigger: car_present == True; action: ev_charger.charging := on
R5 trigger: car_present == True; action: light_garage.power := on
The two rules act on different devices (ev_charger and light_garage)
Both actions turn something on, so they don't contradict each other
Neither action changes car_present or any other value the rules check
The home description doesn't mention a shared circuit or power limit between the charger and the light

explanation: R1 dispenses cat food at 12:00 every day, including when you're out and the home is in away mode, which is exactly when an automatic feeder matters most. Food being dispensed brings the cat running to eat. If the feeder is in or near the kitchen, the kitchen motion sensor will probably detect the cat, and R2 will sound the siren even though there's no intruder. This means you could get a false alarm around noon on any day you're away.
evidence: R1 has no conditions, so it fires at 12:00 whether or not anyone is home, including in away mode.
R1's action (feeder.dispensing := on) is meant to make the cat come to the feeder and eat.
R2 fires on motion_kitchen == True when home_mode == away and turns on alarm.siren.
The home has a cat, so motion in the kitchen while you're away can come from the pet, not only from an intruder.
Assumption: the feeder is in or near the kitchen. The rules don't say where it is, but feeders are usually kept there.
repair: Use a pet-immune motion sensor in the kitchen, or add a condition to R2 that ignores kitchen motion for about 30 minutes after the feeder runs. A second option is to require a second sign of entry before the siren sounds, such as a door or window contact opening. Keep the alarm itself enabled.

explanation: At 12:00, R1 makes the feeder dispense food. The feeder's own movement, or the cat coming over to eat, can set off the kitchen motion sensor. That makes R3 start recording on the kitchen camera at about the same time every day because of an expected pet event, not an intruder. This fills storage with false security clips and can bury real alerts. This only happens if the feeder or the cat's eating spot is where the kitchen motion sensor can see it. The rules don't say where the feeder is, so I'm assuming it's in or near the kitchen.
evidence: R1 runs feeder.dispensing := on every day at 12:00 with no conditions
R3 starts camera_kitchen.recording whenever motion_kitchen == True, with no conditions
The home has a cat and a pet feeder, and the cat will come to the feeder when food is dispensed
The motion sensor can't tell the cat or the feeder's movement apart from a person, so feeding can set off R3
Assumption (not stated in the rules): the feeder or the cat's feeding spot is where the kitchen motion sensor can see it
repair: Add a condition to R3 so it doesn't trigger from feeding. One option is to ignore kitchen motion from 11:55 to 12:30, or only record when nobody is home. Another is to use a pet-immune motion sensor, or person detection on the camera, so the cat doesn't trigger it. Keep the camera and motion sensor working as they do now.

explanation: R4 starts the litter box cleaning at noon, and R5 sounds the siren when the living room detects motion while the home is in away mode. They control different devices, neither rule's action changes the motion sensor or the home mode, and the rules state no physical link between the devices. So neither rule can override, trigger or block the other.
evidence: R4 acts only on litter_box.cleaning; R5 acts only on alarm.siren, so the rules never give opposite commands to the same device.
R5's trigger (motion_living) and condition (home_mode == away) are not changed by any action in R4.
The rules state no shared power supply or other physical link between the litter box and the alarm.
The litter box's location is not given, so it can't be shown that its cleaning cycle is visible to the living-room motion sensor.

explanation: Both rules start when the kitchen detects motion. If the home is in home mode, R3 turns the kitchen camera recording on and R6 turns it off at the same moment. Whether the camera ends up recording depends on which rule runs last, so you can't count on it either for privacy or for security.
evidence: R3 trigger: motion_kitchen == True, no conditions
R6 trigger: motion_kitchen == True, condition home_mode == home
R3 action: camera_kitchen.recording := on
R6 action: camera_kitchen.recording := off
When home_mode == home, both rules fire on the same motion event and set opposite values on camera_kitchen.recording
repair: Add the condition home_mode != home to R3, so it only records when the home is not in home mode. The two rules then never fire together.

explanation: R1 turns off the bedside plug, which is described as the phone charger. R2 turns on the CPAP machine. evidence: R1 only sets plug_bedside.power := off at 23:30, and the plug is described as the phone charger.

evidence: R3 sets lock_entrance.lock := unlocked when fall_detected == True

explanation: These two rules conflict through the room's temperature. At 10:00 R2 opens the living room window, and in summer that lets warm outside air in. explanation: In a server-closet home lab, the NAS is very likely plugged into the closet power strip. Night mode usually starts before 01:00. If it does, R2 cuts power to the strip, so the NAS is already off when R1 tries to start the backup at 01:00 and the backup fails. If night mode starts while a backup is running, R2 cuts power mid-backup, which can corrupt data. The rules never mention this power link, which is why this is a physical conflict.
evidence: The home is described as 'Home lab - server closet cooling', so the NAS most likely sits in the closet and draws power from strip_closet.
R2 sets strip_closet.power := off whenever home_mode switches to night, with no conditions.

Neither rule checks the other: R2 doesn't check whether a backup is running, and R1 doesn't check whether the strip has power.
repair: Plug the NAS (and any closet cooling) into an always-on outlet that R2 doesn't control. If that isn't possible, add a condition to R2 so it only turns off the strip when nas.backup is not running and the time is outside the backup window (for example, after the backup finishes).

R3: when temp_closet > 35, fan_closet.power := on (no conditions)
Both devices are in the same server closet, so the fan is likely powered by the closet strip
R2 has no temperature check and R3 doesn't check that the strip is on, so the fan can be needed while it has no power
repair: Plug the closet fan into an outlet that is always on, not the switched closet strip. If that isn't possible, add a condition to R2 so it only turns off the strip while temp_closet is below about 30 °C. You could also have R3 turn strip_closet.power on before turning the fan on.

explanation: The two rules control different devices: R1 runs the NAS backup and R3 turns on the closet fan, so neither undoes the other. The backup may warm the closet and set off R3, but cooling a hot closet is what R3 is for. Neither rule stops the other from running.

explanation: If the teenager gets home between 23:00 and 06:00, R1 unlocks the front door. That unlock is exactly what triggers R2, which locks the door again straight away. Either way, the door ends up locked at night.

explanation: The two rules control different devices, but they're linked through the room temperature. At 09:00, R1 closes the office shades, which blocks the sun from warming the office. The room can then cool below 20 °C, so R2 turns on the radiator to replace heat the sun would have provided for free. This wastes energy, and the radiator may run on sunny mornings when it otherwise wouldn't need to.
evidence: The home is described as an office with solar heat gain, shades and heating, so the sun warms this room.
R1 sets shades_office.position := closed every day at 09:00 with no conditions, so it closes the shades even when the sun is helping heat the room.
R2 turns radiator_office.mode := heat whenever temp_office < 20, with no other conditions.

repair: Give R1 a temperature check: close the shades fully only when temp_office is 21 °C or higher (or only when there's glare). Otherwise, tilt or partly close them so the sun can still warm the room. Another option is to have R2 skip heating while the shades were closed less than about 30 minutes ago and the outdoor sun is strong.

explanation: R2 and R4 both control the office radiator, but they can never fire at the same time. The office can't be below 20 °C and above 24 °C at once. Between 20 and 24 °C neither rule fires, so the radiator stays as it is. This gap stops it from switching on and off too often. When R2's heating eventually warms the room enough to trigger R4, that's how a thermostat is meant to work, not a conflict.
evidence: R2 trigger: temp_office < 20 -> radiator_office.mode := heat
R4 trigger: temp_office > 24 -> radiator_office.mode := off
The trigger ranges (<20 and >24) don't overlap, so the two rules can't fire together
From 20 to 24 °C neither rule fires, which prevents rapid on/off switching
Heating from R2 can lead to R4 firing later, which is the normal heat-then-stop thermostat cycle

For example, R6 opens the shades at 09:00 only when outdoor light or solar gain is low (e.g. outdoor illuminance below a threshold or cloudy). R1 closes them at 09:00 only when sunlight is strong (glare or heat gain on the screen). Another option is to merge both into one 09:00 rule that picks open or closed based on that light condition.

explanation: R2 starts the white-noise speaker in the nursery at 19:30. That adds sound to the same room where R1 listens for crying above 60 dB. If the white noise is loud enough, or adds to normal background sound so the level goes over 60 dB, R1 will think the baby is crying and turn on the lamp, which could wake the baby. The constant noise can also make it harder to tell real crying apart, so the 60 dB limit stops being a reliable sign that the baby is crying.
evidence: R2 action: white_noise.playing := on in the nursery at 19:30, which adds sound to the room.
R1 trigger: noise_nursery > 60, measured in the same room where the white-noise speaker plays.
R1 has no condition that excludes or adjusts for times when white noise is playing.
Many white-noise machines play at about 50-70 dB near the speaker, which can reach or pass the 60 dB limit, especially when added to other room sounds.
R1 turns on nursery_lamp.power := on, so a false trigger lights up the room while the baby is meant to be sleeping.
repair: Add a condition to R1 so that while white_noise.playing == on, the lamp only turns on when noise_nursery goes above a higher limit set from the measured white-noise level (for example, about 10 dB above it). Alternatively, use a cry-detection signal from the baby monitor instead of the raw sound level. Also keep the white-noise volume clearly below 60 dB at the sensor.

explanation: After 20:00, R3 turns on the soundbar whenever the TV turns on, and the extra sound can raise the noise level picked up in the nursery. R1 treats any nursery noise above 60 dB as a crying baby, so loud TV audio could turn on the nursery lamp falsely, at bedtime, and possibly wake the baby. How likely this is depends on how well sound travels from the TV room to the nursery, which the rules don't say.
evidence: R3 action soundbar.power := on adds a new sound source in the home
R3 runs in the evening/night window 20:00-23:59, which is typically baby bedtime
R1 trigger is just noise_nursery > 60 dB and doesn't check where the noise comes from
R1 has no conditions (no time, duration or source check), so any loud sound reaching the nursery fires it
60 dB is roughly the level of normal conversation or TV sound, so audio leaking from the soundbar could plausibly cross it
R1's action turns on a light in the nursery, which could disturb a sleeping baby if it fires falsely
repair: Make R1's cry detection stricter without turning it off: require noise_nursery > 60 dB for at least 10-15 seconds, and while the soundbar is on, only fire if the nursery reading is clearly louder than the TV-room level or the baby monitor's own cry detection confirms it. Optionally, cap the soundbar volume after 20:00.

explanation: These two rules control different devices. R4 turns the TV off and R2 turns on the nursery white-noise speaker. Neither rule changes something the other one depends on: turning off the TV doesn't stop the speaker from starting at 19:30, and the speaker doesn't change the home mode. Even if both run around the same time, they work together and don't clash.
evidence: R4 acts only on tv.power (sets it to off).
R2 acts only on white_noise.playing (sets it to on).

explanation: During a frost warning, R1 turns the heater on. Nothing tells the heater when to stop, so it can warm the greenhouse past 18 °C, which triggers R2 and opens the roof vent. Freezing outside air then comes in while the heater keeps running. That wastes energy, can expose plants to cold drafts, and makes the two devices work against each other.
evidence: R1 sets gh_heater.power := on whenever frost_warning == True, with no conditions and no temperature limit.
R2 sets gh_vent.position := open whenever temp_gh > 18, with no conditions.
Running the heater raises temp_gh, the same value that triggers R2.
R2 does not check frost_warning or whether the heater is on, so the vent can open during a frost warning.
An open roof vent lets heat escape and cold air in, which undoes what R1 is trying to do.
repair: Add a condition to R2 so the vent only opens when frost_warning == False and gh_heater.power == off. Also give R1 a temperature limit: turn the heater off when temp_gh reaches about 15 °C, which keeps it below the 18 °C vent threshold.

explanation: In a garden greenhouse the heater is often powered from the outdoor socket. If gh_heater is plugged into plug_outdoor, R3 cuts its power at 22:00 even after R1 has turned it on for a frost warning. Frost risk is highest at night, so the plants would lose heat when they need it most, and the heater would still show as 'on' in the system. If the heater is on a separate circuit, there is no conflict.
evidence: R1 sets gh_heater.power := on when frost_warning == True, with no time restriction.
R3 sets plug_outdoor.power := off every day at 22:00, with no conditions (it does not check for a frost warning or the heater's state).
The home is a garden greenhouse, where the heater is commonly powered from an outdoor socket. The rules do not say which outlet the heater uses.
Frost warnings usually apply overnight, so R1 is likely to be active at 22:00 when R3 fires.
repair: Add the conditions 'frost_warning == False AND gh_heater.power == off' to R3 so the outdoor plug is never switched off while the heater needs power. Alternatively, move the heater onto a circuit that the 22:00 shut-off does not control.

explanation: R4 turns on the grow lights at 06:00 and R2 opens the roof vent when the greenhouse is warmer than 18 °C. They control different devices and never give opposite commands. Heat from the lights may help trigger the vent, but venting a warm greenhouse is exactly what R2 is for, so neither rule works against the other.
evidence: R4 acts only on grow_lights.power (on) at 06:00.
R2 acts only on gh_vent.position (open) when temp_gh > 18.
No device is controlled by both rules, so no opposite commands are possible.
Neither action cuts power to or blocks the device used by the other rule.
Heat from the grow lights can raise temp_gh, which fits R2's purpose of venting a warm greenhouse.

If opening the vent cools the greenhouse down to 5 °C, R5 closes it, which is what R5 is for. The 13 °C gap between the thresholds also stops the vent from flapping open and shut.

R5 trigger: temp_gh < 5 -> gh_vent.position := closed

explanation: During a frost warning, R1 turns the heater on with no stop condition, so the greenhouse can go above 18 °C. R2 opens the vent (gh_vent.position := open) whenever the greenhouse is above 18 °C (temp_gh > 18), whatever the weather outside.

R3 only switches off plug_outdoor at 22:00. The rules don't say the heater or vent is powered by that plug, so R3 isn't part of this conflict. If either one is plugged into it, R3 would also cut its power at night during a frost.

explanation: R1 turns the greenhouse heater on when a frost warning comes in, and R6 turns it off at 22:00 every night no matter what. R1 only runs when a warning is first issued, so the heater stays off for the rest of the frosty night.
evidence: R1 sets gh_heater.power := on when frost_warning == True
R6 sets gh_heater.power := off at time == 22:00 and has no conditions
Both rules control the same device state (gh_heater.power) in opposite directions
A frost warning can still be active at 22:00, since frost risk is highest at night
R1 runs when the warning starts, so nothing turns the heater back on after R6 switches it off
repair: Add a condition to R6 so it only turns the heater off at 22:00 if frost_warning == False. That way the heater keeps running through the night while a frost warning is active.

explanation: R1 turns off the hallway smart plug every night at 23:00 to save energy, no matter what mode the home is in. If the hallway camera gets its power from that plug, which is a common setup for a hallway security camera though the rules don't say so, the camera loses power at 23:00. R2 can still switch recording on when the home is set to away, but the camera won't actually record. You would then have no hallway footage at night while you're away, and neither rule warns you.

explanation: R3 locks the front door when the home goes into night mode. R4 unlocks the same door whenever there's motion in the hallway between 22:00 and 06:00. explanation: These two rules don't conflict. R5 turns off the living room lamp at 23:00. R2 starts recording on the hallway camera when the home switches to away mode. explanation: R1 turns on the living room heater at 18:00. No rule turns it off and it has no temperature limit, so the room keeps warming. evidence: R2 sets window_living.position := open and vent_living.power := on when temp_living > 26

explanation: R1 and R5 both run at 18:00 and control the same living room heater. R1 has no conditions, so when the home is in away mode both rules fire together: R1 turns the heater on and R5 turns it off. Whichever command arrives last decides the result. evidence: R1 trigger: time == 18:00, with no conditions
R5 trigger: time == 18:00, with condition home_mode == away
R1 action: heater_living.power := on
R5 action: heater_living.power := off
Both rules control the same device and state (heater_living.power) at the same moment whenever home_mode == away

explanation: At 10:00, R1 starts the robot vacuum. When the vacuum drives through the living room, the motion sensor can pick it up. R2 treats that motion as proof that someone is home and unlocks the front door. On a weekday morning the house is probably empty, so the front door could end up unlocked with nobody there.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 (intended for weekdays), when residents are typically away.
A robot vacuum moving through the living room can trigger the motion_living sensor.
R2 fires on motion_living == True with no conditions and sets lock_entrance.lock := unlocked.

explanation: R1 starts the robot vacuum at 10:00 on weekdays, when the home is often in away mode. As the vacuum moves through the living room, it can set off the motion sensor there. R3 then sees motion while the home is away and sounds the alarm, even though nobody is inside.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 on weekdays, with no condition about who is home

A moving robot vacuum can trigger a living-room motion sensor (motion_living == True)

explanation: When the robot vacuum starts cleaning at 10:00 (R1), it moves through the house. When it passes through the bedroom, it can set off the bedroom motion sensor. R4 then turns on the entrance light even though no one is there. This wastes energy and gives a false sign that someone is home.
evidence: R1 sets vacuum.mode := cleaning at 10:00 with no conditions, so the vacuum moves around the house.
R4 is triggered by motion_bedroom == True and has no conditions that rule out the vacuum or check whether anyone is home.

explanation: R1 unlocks the apartment door when kitchen smoke is detected so people can get out. R2 locks the same door whenever the home switches to away mode, and it doesn't check for smoke. evidence: R1 sets lock_door.lock := unlocked when smoke_kitchen == True

Both rules act on the same device (lock_door) with opposite values
R2 has no condition that stops it while smoke is present, so it can fire during an active smoke event
Neither rule has a condition that rules out the other, so the final lock state depends on which one fires last

explanation: R1 turns the air handler off when smoke is detected in the kitchen. R4 turns it back on at 08:00 every day and doesn't check for smoke. If smoke is still present at 08:00, R4 overrides R1's safety shutdown, and the air handler could spread smoke through the apartment.
evidence: R1 action: hvac.power := off when smoke_kitchen == True
R4 action: hvac.power := on at time == 08:00

explanation: When a frost warning comes in, R1 turns on the heater. Nothing in R1 sets a temperature limit, so the heater can push the greenhouse above 18 °C. That makes R2 open the roof vent on a frosty night, and cold air comes in while the heater keeps running. This wastes energy and the cold air works against the frost protection. Also, R2 never closes the vent again on its own.
evidence: R1 turns on gh_heater when frost_warning == True and has no temperature limit or setpoint
R2 opens gh_vent whenever temp_gh > 18 and has no conditions
The heater raises temp_gh, so R1's action can make R2 fire
R2 does not check frost_warning or whether the heater is on, so the vent can open during a frost warning
No rule closes the vent, so it can stay open while cold air comes in
repair: Add a condition to R2 so it only opens the vent when frost_warning == False and gh_heater.power == off. Also give the heater a thermostat setpoint below 18 °C, for example turn it off above 12 °C.

explanation: These two rules can probably conflict, but only if the heater runs off the outdoor plug. The rules don't say how the heater gets power. In a garden greenhouse it's likely plugged into the outdoor smart plug. If so, the 22:00 power-off in R3 would cut the heater's power even after R1 has switched it on for a frost warning. The heater would still read 'on' but give no heat, right when frost is most likely.
evidence: The home is a garden greenhouse with heating, vents and grow lights, so its devices are likely powered from an outdoor supply.
R3 turns plug_outdoor off at 22:00 every night, with no conditions.
R1 turns gh_heater on when frost_warning == True, with no conditions.
Frost warnings usually cover the night, so they overlap with the 22:00 power cut.
R3 doesn't check whether a frost warning is active or whether the heater is running. Nothing turns the plug back on if a warning comes in after 22:00.
Assumption: the heater gets its power through plug_outdoor. This isn't stated in the rules.
repair: Add a condition to R3: frost_warning == False AND gh_heater.power == off. Also add plug_outdoor.power := on to R1's actions so the heater has power when a frost warning comes in after 22:00. If the heater isn't on the outdoor plug, these rules don't conflict.

If that pushes it above 18 °C, R2 opens the vent, which is exactly what R2 is meant to do whatever the heat source. Neither rule stops the other from working, and there is no hidden power or physical link between the two devices.
evidence: R4 only sets grow_lights.power := on at 06:00
R2 only sets gh_vent.position := open when temp_gh > 18
The two rules act on different devices (grow_lights vs gh_vent), so they can't issue opposite commands
Any warming from the grow lights only makes R2 open the vent at its own 18 °C setpoint, which is the intended cooling behaviour
R2 never changes the light level or the time, so it can't trigger R4 or stop it from running

The 5–18 °C gap between them works as a buffer, so the vent won't keep flipping open and shut. If opening the vent ever cooled the greenhouse below 5 °C, R5 closing it would be the intended protective response, not an unexpected side effect.

R3 is not part of this conflict unless the heater is wired to the outdoor plug, which the rules don't say.

R3 only controls plug_outdoor, and nothing in the rules links that plug to the heater or vent
